extra.message: Forgeable session token allows authentication bypass / privilege escalation — Attacker forges a session cookie to impersonate any user (e.g. admin) without credentials [verified: dashboard() at line 111 decodes the cookie and trusts the embedded username with zero signature/HMAC verification, so any base64('admin:...') string grants admin impersonation.]

Insecure deserialization via pickle.loads on user-controlled input — Remote code execution on the lab server by submitting a malicious pickle payload to /deserialize [verified: deserialize_data() calls pickle.loads() directly on attacker-supplied base64 data at line 36 with no validation, signing, or restricted unpickler; the isinstance check happens only after unpickling has already executed any __reduce__ payload.]

Unauthenticated endpoint exposes all users' sensitive data — Any unauthenticated attacker can retrieve every registered user's credit card number, SSN, and API key via GET /api/all-users/, enabling mass identity theft/credential harvesting. [verified: all_users_data_view has no auth decorator or check and returns all users' credit_card, ssn, and api_key in plaintext to anyone.]

Missing authorization on endpoint exposing all users' sensitive data — Any unauthenticated attacker can dump every user's credit card number, SSN, and API key [verified: Same endpoint/root cause as idx0 - confirmed missing authorization allowing full data dump.]

Code injection via eval() in mitre.py — Arbitrary Python code execution [verified: expression comes directly from request.POST with no validation and is passed to eval(), and the endpoint is csrf_exempt with no auth decorator.]

OS command injection in mitre.py — Arbitrary OS command execution [verified: ip is concatenated unsanitized into a shell string run via subprocess.Popen(shell=True), allowing command injection; endpoint is csrf_exempt with no auth check.]

SQL Injection in SQL lab — Attacker can bypass authentication, extract/modify arbitrary DB data via classic UNION/boolean SQLi [verified: same as idx4, name/password concatenated into raw SQL via login.objects.raw().]

Insecure Deserialization via pickle in cookie token — Attacker crafts a malicious pickle payload as the token cookie to achieve remote code execution. [verified: token cookie is base64-decoded and passed directly to pickle.loads with no validation.]
OS command injection in nslookup/dig lab — Arbitrary OS command execution on the server as the app user [verified: same command injection as idx0 via subprocess.Popen(command, shell=True).]

OS command injection in nslookup/dig lab — Arbitrary OS command execution on the server via shell metacharacters in the domain field [verified: duplicate of idx0/13, command injection via shell=True Popen.]
Arbitrary Code Execution via eval() on user input — Full RCE via payloads like __import__('os').system('id'). [verified: val is passed directly to eval() with no sandboxing.]

Unsafe YAML Load (yaml.Loader) Enables RCE — Attacker uploads a crafted YAML file to achieve remote code execution during deserialization. [verified: uploaded file is parsed with yaml.load(file, yaml.Loader), the unsafe loader.]
SQL Injection in A3 injection lab — Full SQL injection allowing data exfiltration/auth bypass [verified: same as idx5, id/password concatenated into raw SQL via sql_lab_table.objects.raw().]

SQL Injection in A3 injection lab — Auth bypass / arbitrary row disclosure via classic SQLi payloads. [verified: id/password concatenated into raw SQL executed via sql_lab_table.objects.raw() with no parameterization.]

No rate limiting / plaintext password storage enabling brute force — Attacker can brute-force credentials with unlimited attempts; compromised DB yields plaintext passwords directly [verified: login() does plaintext comparison (line 41) and registration stores plaintext passwords (line 68) with no rate limiting, lockout, or hashing anywhere in the file.]

Predictable password-reset token disclosed in HTTP response — Attacker requests a reset for a victim's email and receives the reset token directly in the response, allowing full account takeover [verified: reset_password() flashes the raw token in the HTTP response (line 91) instead of emailing it, and the token itself is a guessable md5(email:timestamp), enabling full account takeover.]

Hardcoded/weak JWT signing secret in CSRF lab — Attacker can forge valid session JWTs for arbitrary usernames, achieving full account takeover on the CSRF lab [verified: jwt.encode/decode both use the hardcoded literal 'csrf_vulneribility' at lines 169/182/194 with no secret rotation or config lookup, letting anyone who reads the source forge tokens for any username.]

CSRF via state-changing GET request in money transfer API — Attacker can force an authenticated victim's browser to transfer funds to an attacker-controlled account without consent [verified: csrf_transfer_monei_api performs a state-changing balance transfer on GET with only JWT cookie auth and no CSRF token check; browsers auto-send cookies, so an attacker tag exploits this cross-site.]

Server-Side Template Injection via blog lab (no-op sanitizer) — Attacker-controlled Django template tags/filters execute server-side; can be leveraged to read internal template context/settings and chain with template tag abuse for further compromise [verified: filter_blog() is a no-op (introduction/utility.py:55-56) so attacker-controlled `blog` POST data flows unsanitized into a template file that ssti_view_blog renders via Django's template engine (views.py:981-1006), giving full server-side DTL execution.]
XXE via explicitly enabled external entity resolution — Arbitrary local file disclosure or SSRF via crafted XML external entities [verified: duplicate of idx8, XXE via feature_external_ges.]

Session/account takeover via unsigned sequential userid cookie — Attacker can enumerate small integer userid values and hijack any registered account without credentials. [verified: auth_lab_login GET path authenticates solely via client-supplied sequential userid cookie with no signing.]

Authorization bypass via spoofable client header — Unauthenticated/any user can obtain the 'S3CR37K3Y' secret by spoofing an HTTP header. [verified: secret() authorizes purely on the attacker-controlled X-Host header with no real auth check.]

Code injection via ImageMath.eval in A9 lab2 — Arbitrary Python expression evaluation potentially leading to RCE depending on ImageMath's eval implementation and available names [verified: function_str from POST passed directly to ImageMath.eval with no allowlist.]

Path Traversal / Local File Disclosure in blog reader — Attacker supplies '../../../../etc/passwd' or app source/settings.py (leaking SECRET_KEY) as the blog parameter to read arbitrary files. [verified: blog POST param is joined via os.path.join and opened with no traversal sanitization.]

SSRF via unrestricted requests.get on user-supplied URL — Attacker reaches internal-only services or cloud metadata endpoints (e.g. 169.254.169.254) and exfiltrates the response via the app. [verified: url from POST is passed directly to requests.get with no allow-listing and response content is reflected.]

Hardcoded Django SECRET_KEY — Knowledge of SECRET_KEY allows forging session cookies and signed tokens, enabling authentication bypass/account takeover. [verified: SECRET_KEY is hardcoded and committed to source, used for session signing; genuinely absent secret management on a reachable, always-used path.]

DEBUG=True in shipped settings — Unhandled exceptions leak full stack traces, source snippets, local variables, and configuration details to any user. [verified: DEBUG=True with no env override is shipped in settings.py, exposing full stack traces/config on any unhandled exception.]

Hardcoded weak JWT signing secret — Attacker forges a JWT with an admin claim using the known secret to gain unauthorized admin-only access. [verified: SECRET_COOKIE_KEY is trivially guessable and used to sign/verify JWTs, letting an attacker forge tokens with arbitrary claims.]

Unbounded Docker container spawning enables resource-exhaustion DoS — An authenticated low-privilege user can exhaust host resources (CPU, memory, available ports, Docker daemon capacity) by triggering many container launches, degrading or crashing the service for all users. [verified: No limit on concurrent containers or ports per user/global is visible in challenge/views.py, so repeated POSTs by an authenticated user can exhaust host resources/ports; this is a genuine missing-control DoS.]

Weak MD5-derived password reset token — Attacker can predict or brute-force password reset tokens and take over accounts [verified: Token = MD5(email:timestamp) with known email and coarse-grained timestamp is guessable/brute-forceable, and no rate limiting or single-use enforcement exists on /reset/<token>, enabling account takeover.]

Hardcoded Flask secret key and debug mode enabled — Remote code execution via the Werkzeug debugger if exposed, plus forgeable signed cookies from the known static secret key [verified: Static secret_key (line 8) and debug=True (line 122) are both present with no override, enabling RCE via Werkzeug debugger and forgeable Flask-signed data if reachable.]

Sensitive PII (full credit card/SSN) exposed unmasked in API response — Full credit card number and SSN disclosed in API responses, usable for fraud if session/cookies are stolen [verified: api_data_view requires login but returns unmasked credit card and SSN for the session's own user, a real sensitive-data-exposure pattern even though scoped to self, so severity is lower than the unauthenticated mass-exposure findings.]

Hardcoded Django SECRET_KEY and DEBUG=True in sensitive_data_exposure lab — Session/CSRF token forgery via known SECRET_KEY; verbose debug pages leak source code, settings, and stack traces to attackers [verified: settings.py confirmed hardcodes SECRET_KEY='django-insecure-key-for-demonstration-only' with DEBUG=True and ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'], no environment override present in this file.]

Weak unsalted MD5 password hashing in CSRF lab login — Leaked password hashes can be reversed via rainbow tables, exposing plaintext user credentials [verified: Line 161 hashes the password with unsalted md5 before the DB comparison, with no pepper/salt or modern KDF anywhere in the flow.]

Broken access control via client-controlled trust cookie — Any authenticated (non-admin) user can forge the 'admin' cookie to access admin-only secret data, bypassing the password check entirely. [verified: admin cookie is a plain client-controlled value with no signing or session binding, checked to grant admin secret.]
Weak/predictable OTP generation — Attacker can brute-force the 3-digit OTP to bypass the verification step [verified: duplicate of idx20, weak PRNG for OTP generation.]

OTP lab trusts client-controlled email cookie for identity — Account takeover by pairing a spoofed email cookie with a brute-forced OTP [verified: OTP verification identifies user solely via client-controlled email cookie with no server-side binding.]

Server-side template injection via blog content — Arbitrary server-side template execution, potentially leading to RCE or sensitive data disclosure via Django template tags [verified: duplicate of idx9, SSTI via blog content written to rendered template.]

Unvalidated path parameter used to select template file — Depending on Django template loader search paths, a crafted blog_id could attempt to load/render other .html templates in configured template directories [verified: blog_id path param is interpolated directly into the template path with no identifier validation, though Django's loader restricts to configured template dirs limiting full traversal impact.]

Server-Side Template Injection via user blog rendered as Django template — Attacker injects Django Template Language directives to manipulate rendered pages or achieve information disclosure/RCE through insufficiently blocked tags/filters. [verified: filter_blog is a blocklist that doesn't cover all DTL constructs, and content is written to a real template file and rendered by Django's engine.]

Account enumeration via password reset response — Attacker can enumerate which email addresses are registered accounts, aiding targeted credential-stuffing/phishing attacks [verified: reset_password() returns a distinct 'Email not found' message (line 94) versus the reset-link message for valid emails, allowing trivial account enumeration.]

Permissive ALLOWED_HOSTS wildcard — Enables Host header injection attacks such as poisoned password-reset links or cache poisoning [verified: ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*'] disables Django's Host header validation for this lab's app with no compensating control present in this settings file. Severity is low since this is an isolated intentionally-vulnerable demo lab, not production infrastructure.]

MD5 used for password hashing — Attacker with DB access can crack passwords rapidly via rainbow tables or GPU brute force due to MD5's speed and lack of salting design intent. [verified: password is hashed with unsalted MD5 for authentication comparison.]

Weak unsalted MD5 used for password comparison — MD5 is fast and unsalted, enabling trivial rainbow-table/brute-force recovery of user passwords from the DB [verified: duplicate of idx10, unsalted MD5 used for password comparison.]
